Teacher Model Answers and Marking Rubric
Teacher reference material. Use the exact question IDs and maximum marks.
Q1 — Maximum 5 marks
Question: Explain what a database is and state two benefits of using a database.
Model answer: A database is an organized collection of related data. Benefits include easier retrieval,
reduced duplication, improved consistency, controlled access, and reliable sharing.
Marking rubric: Definition of organized related data: 2; One valid benefit: 1; Second distinct valid benefit: 1;
Relevance and clarity: 1
Q2(a) — Maximum 3 marks
Question: Define a primary key in a relational database.
Model answer: A primary key is a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row in a table. Its
values must be unique and cannot be NULL.
Marking rubric: Uniquely identifies a row: 2; Mentions uniqueness and/or non-NULL: 1
Q3 — Maximum 4 marks
Question: What is a foreign key? State its purpose.
Model answer: A foreign key is a column or set of columns that refers to a key in another or the same
table. It establishes relationships and helps maintain referential integrity.
Marking rubric: References a key in another/same table: 2; Explains table relationships: 1; Mentions
referential integrity: 1
Q4 — Maximum 5 marks
Question: Explain database normalization and give one reason it is useful.
Model answer: Normalization organizes data into related tables to reduce duplication and improve
integrity. It can reduce insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.
Marking rubric: Organizes/decomposes data into related tables: 2; Explains reducing redundancy: 1; Valid
benefit such as integrity/fewer anomalies: 2
Q5 — Maximum 5 marks
Question: Differentiate between a primary key and a foreign key.
Model answer: A primary key uniquely identifies a row in its own table. A foreign key references a key in
another or the same table to create relationships and maintain referential integrity.
Marking rubric: Correct primary-key explanation: 2; Correct foreign-key explanation: 2; Meaningful
difference/purpose: 1

tests.question:
COMPUTER NETWORKS
Assignment Question Paper
Maximum Marks: 50 Duration: 2 Hours
General Instructions
1. Attempt all questions.
2. Marks are indicated against each question.
3. Show all working for numerical problems.
Q1. [6 Marks]
A LAN has a rated bandwidth of 10 Mbps. During a measurement interval, the network was
observed to carry 12,000 frames per minute, where each frame is 10,000 bits long.
(a) Calculate the total number of bits transmitted per minute. [2]
(b) Compute the effective throughput of the LAN in bps and in Mbps. [2]
(c) Explain why the measured throughput is lower than the rated bandwidth of 10 Mbps. [2]
Q2. [7 Marks]
The following UDP header was captured in hexadecimal:
CB84 000D 001C 001C
(a) Separate the header into its hexadecimal byte pairs and identify the four UDP header
fields. [2]
(b) Determine the source port, destination port, UDP length and checksum values (give
decimal values where applicable). [3]
(c) Given that the UDP header is 8 bytes long, calculate the size of the UDP data. [1]
(d) State the byte order used for port fields and explain what the Length field represents. [1]
Q3. [5 Marks]
An organisation is allocated the IP block 17.63.110.114/24.
(a) Write the subnet mask and the network address of the block. [1]
(b) Determine the first usable address, the last usable address and the broadcast address. [3]
(c) State the valid host range and explain the role of the first and last addresses of the block.
[1]
Q4. [6 Marks]
Draw the layered structure of the TCP/IP model (top to bottom) and briefly explain the function
of each layer: Application Layer, Transport Layer, Network Layer and Data Link Layer.
Q5. [6 Marks]
(a) Describe the Stop-and-Wait protocol and explain why it is inefficient when the round-trip
time (RTT) is large compared with the frame transmission time. [2]
(b) Write the formula for link utilization (U) in Stop-and-Wait. [1]
(c) Explain how Selective Repeat ARQ overcomes these inefficiencies. [3]
Q6. [4 Marks]
Explain the working of the Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) error-detection technique. Describe
how the sender computes the check value, how the receiver detects an error, and state the
practical result of using CRC.
Q7. [5 Marks]
Compare IPv4 and IPv6 on the following bases:
(a) Address size [1]
(b) Header and options [2]
(c) Built-in features [2]
Q8. [5 Marks]
Explain how the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) works. Your answer should
cover:
(a) The role of the DHCP server and its address pool [1]
(b) The DORA process [2]
(c) The use of an ARP probe before address assignment [1]
(d) The role of lease expiration [1]
Q9. [6 Marks]
(a) Compare TCP and UDP in terms of connection type, reliability, ordering, latency and
overhead. [3]
(b) For each of the following applications, recommend a suitable transport protocol and
justify your choice: [3]
(i) Real-time streaming, online gaming and VoIP
(ii) On-demand video (e.g., Netflix, YouTube)
— End of Question Paper —
tests.model_answer:
COMPUTER NETWORKS
Assignment – Model Answer Sheet
Maximum Marks: 50
Q1. [6 Marks]
Given
• LAN bandwidth = 10 Mbps
• Measured traffic = 12,000 frames/min, each frame = 10,000 bits
(a) Total bits per minute [2]
12,000 × 10,000 = 120,000,000 bits
(b) Throughput [2]
120,000,000 / 60 = 2,000,000 bps = 2 Mbps
(c) Why it is lower than 10 Mbps [2]
• Protocol overhead, collisions and retransmissions
• Limits in application or host processing
• Congestion or queuing delays
• Errors and retransmission reduce the effective throughput
Q2. [7 Marks]
(a) Byte pairs and fields [2]
CB 84 | 00 0D | 00 1C | 00 1C
The four fields are: Source Port, Destination Port, Length and Checksum.
(b) Field values [3]
• Source port = 0xCB84 = 52100 (decimal)
• Destination port = 0x000D = 13
• Length (total UDP length) = 0x001C = 28 bytes
• Checksum = 0x001C (28 in decimal)
(c) Size of UDP data [1]
UDP header = 8 bytes, so data size = 28 − 8 = 20 bytes.
(d) Byte order and Length field [1]
• Ports are 16-bit fields stored in network byte order (big-endian).
• Length is the length of the entire UDP datagram (header + data).
Q3. [5 Marks]
(a) Mask and network address [1]
For /24 the subnet mask is 255.255.255.0 and the network address is 17.63.110.0.
(b) Usable and broadcast addresses [3]
• First usable address: 17.63.110.1
• Last usable address: 17.63.110.254
• Broadcast address: 17.63.110.255
(c) Host range [1]
Host range is .1 through .254; .0 is the network address and .255 is the broadcast address.
Q4. [6 Marks]
TCP/IP layers (top to bottom)
Application Layer ↓ Transport Layer ↓ Network Layer ↓ Data Link
Layer
Application Layer
• Process-to-process communication
• Application-specific semantics (e.g., SMTP mail delivery rules)
Transport Layer
• Reliable byte-stream delivery (TCP), ensuring in-order delivery
• Multiplexing/demultiplexing using ports, allowing many applications to share the
network
Network Layer
• Routing: finding a path between source and destination across the network
• Logical addressing (IP addressing) and fragmentation
Data Link Layer
• Frame transmission and media access
• Error detection at frame level
Q5. [6 Marks]
(a) Stop-and-Wait and its inefficiency [2]
• The sender transmits one frame and then waits for the ACK.
• If the Round-Trip Time (RTT) is large compared with the frame transmission time, the
channel stays idle for most of the time.
(b) Link utilization [1]
U = Frame transmission time / (Frame transmission time + RTT)
(c) Selective Repeat ARQ [3]
• The sender can transmit multiple frames at once (sliding window).
• Only the erroneous frames are retransmitted, not the whole sequence.
• This increases throughput and utilization, especially on long-delay links.
Q6. [4 Marks]
• CRC computes the remainder of the polynomial division of the data by a generator
polynomial.
• The remainder is appended to the data as the checksum.
• The receiver divides the received bits by the same generator; a non-zero remainder means
an error is detected.
• Practical result: it detects burst errors and many random errors with high probability.
Q7. [5 Marks]
(a) Address size [1]
IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses; IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.
(b) Header and options [2]
IPv6 has a simplified header and uses extension headers for options, which gives faster routing.
(c) Built-in features [2]
IPv6 supports autoconfiguration and eliminates the need for NAT; this affects addressing and
routing.
Q8. [5 Marks]
(a) DHCP server and pool [1]
• The DHCP server manages a pool of IP addresses.
• When a client requests one, the server leases an unused address.
(b) DORA [2]
Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge
(c) ARP probe [1]
Before assignment, DHCP may send an ARP probe to confirm the address is not already in use.
(d) Lease expiration [1]
Lease expiration is used to reclaim addresses.
Q9. [6 Marks]
(a) TCP vs UDP [3]
• TCP (connection-oriented): reliable and ordered, but higher latency (retransmissions,
head-of-line blocking).
• UDP (connectionless): faster with minimal overhead, but no reliability.
(b) Recommendations [3]
• Real-time streaming / gaming / VoIP → UDP, because speed matters more than perfect
reliability.
• On-demand video (Netflix, YouTube) → TCP/HTTP.
— End of Answer Sheet —

● Grayscale conversion — OCR performs better on grayscale images than on raw colour
images.

as characters.

background, sharpening the boundary between ink and paper.

isolating just the answer sheet.

more reliable.

algorithms such as edge detection, filtering, thresholding, and contour detection.

1. Abstract
Manually grading handwritten assignments is slow and inconsistent: a teacher with a large class may
spend eight to ten hours reading, interpreting handwriting, judging correctness, and writing
feedback for a single assignment. This document presents the research and design for an AI-
powered assignment evaluation platform that automates this workflow end to end. The system
accepts a photograph of a handwritten answer, cleans it using classical computer vision techniques,
converts the handwriting to machine-readable text using deep-learning-based Optical Character
Recognition (OCR), and then uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to semantically compare the
student's answer against a model answer, producing marks and constructive feedback within
seconds. The complete platform is built on the MERN stack (MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, Node.js)
and exposes separate dashboards for teachers and students.
2. Introduction and Problem Statement
In a typical classroom of about 100 students, a teacher must read every submitted answer sheet,
decipher individual handwriting styles, judge whether the answer is conceptually correct, assign
marks, and write feedback for each student. This process is repetitive, time-consuming, and prone to
inconsistency between different graders or even the same grader across a long session.
The goal of this project is to replace this manual process with an AI Tutor that can perform the same
evaluation automatically: a student uploads a photograph of their handwritten answer, and within
seconds the system returns marks and detailed feedback. This reduces teacher workload
significantly while giving students faster, more consistent feedback on their work.
3. Objectives
● Automate the evaluation of handwritten assignments from image capture to final feedback.
● Apply classical computer vision techniques to clean noisy, tilted, or poorly lit handwritten
images before recognition.
● Use a deep-learning OCR model to accurately convert handwriting into digital text.
● Use a Large Language Model to semantically evaluate the extracted answer against a
teacher-provided model answer, rather than relying on rigid keyword matching.
● Generate marks and human-readable feedback automatically and store them for later
review.
● Provide separate, role-based dashboards for teachers and students built on the MERN stack.

5. Module 1 — Image Preprocessing with OpenCV
A photograph taken by a student's phone is rarely clean: it may suffer from poor lighting, shadows,
tilt, blur, or background noise. OCR accuracy depends heavily on image quality, so the first stage of
the pipeline uses OpenCV — a computer vision library, not a machine learning model — to prepare
the image.
5.1 Preprocessing Steps
● Grayscale conversion — OCR performs better on grayscale images than on raw colour
images.
● Noise removal — eliminates small artefacts (specks, dust, stray marks) that could be misread
as characters.
● Thresholding (binarisation) — converts the image into pure black text on a white
background, sharpening the boundary between ink and paper.
● Deskewing — straightens a photo taken at an angle so text lines are horizontal.
● Cropping — removes irrelevant background such as the desk, hands, or other objects,
isolating just the answer sheet.
● Line segmentation — separates the answer into individual lines to make downstream OCR
more reliable.
It is worth clarifying that OpenCV itself is not machine learning; it applies classical image-processing
algorithms such as edge detection, filtering, thresholding, and contour detection.
6. Module 2 — Optical Character Recognition (OCR)
Once the image is cleaned, OCR converts the handwritten content into machine-readable text.
Unlike OpenCV, modern OCR engines are themselves deep-learning models, trained on large
datasets of handwritten samples, and therefore qualify as AI.
